one_liner: Alibaba's stackful-coroutine C++ I/O runtime (epoll/io_uring/kqueue); its echo server beats boost::asio on single-core QPS.
what_it_does: Photon replaces callback-style async I/O with lightweight user-space 'photon threads' (stackful coroutines) scheduled M:1 on each OS thread, which it calls a vCPU. You write blocking-style code, such as a per-connection loop of sock->read()/sock->write(); a call that would block parks the coroutine until the event engine wakes it. The API is not asio's: you call photon::init(), start coroutines with thread_create11() or photon_std::thread, and serve through ISocketServer/ISocketStream (new_tcp_socket_server() etc.) using coroutine-aware mutex, semaphore and channel. It is a whole 'libOS', not just an event loop: it also provides file I/O (libaio, io_uring), HTTP client/server, RPC, TLS, and filesystem and cache layers.
how_it_is_fast: The context switch uses context-aware context switching (CACS), described in the project's 'Stackful Coroutine Made Fast' paper. The x86-64 assembly saves only rbp and rsp, and the inline-asm call lists every other register as clobbered, so the compiler spills only the registers that are live at that call site. Each vCPU keeps a private, lock-free run queue (an intrusive list) and a min-heap sleep queue. The epoll, io_uring and kqueue backends register one-shot interests whose event data is the waiting coroutine's pointer, so an event wakes it through thread_interrupt() with no lookup. Sockets are non-blocking and try the syscall first, waiting only on EAGAIN (doio_once in net/basic_socket.h). Optional io_uring sockets, zero-copy send and F-Stack/DPDK backends sit behind the same interface.
when_to_use: Moving thread-per-connection or blocking-style C++ server or storage code to high concurrency without rewriting it into callbacks. photon_std::thread, mutex and condition_variable are namespace-swap replacements for the std:: versions.

Linux TCP services where one core pushes a few high-throughput streams (multiplexed RPC or HTTP/2-like traffic): Photon's page shows about 2.5x boost::asio's per-core QPS in its 512-byte streaming echo test.
Storage or data-plane services that mix network and disk I/O (libaio/O_DIRECT, io_uring) and want one scheduler for both. This is its production origin at Alibaba Cloud storage (overlaybd, OSSFSv2).
You want to try io_uring, zero-copy TCP, RDMA (SMC-R/rsocket) or F-Stack/DPDK and SPDK backends without changing application code, since they sit behind the same socket and file interfaces.
Linux or macOS on x86-64 or ARM64, built with GCC 8-14 or Clang in C++14 or later.
when_not_to_use: Windows or RISC-V targets. The README lists only Linux and macOS; IOCP and MinGW code exists, but Windows support is still an open request (#396) and RISC-V is an open question (#1094).
You depend on the asio ecosystem (Beast, strands, completion tokens, C++20 awaitables, executors). Photon has no asio compatibility layer, so switching means a rewrite of the I/O layer.
Clients that must verify TLS certificates: open issue #457 says Photon's TLS adaptors do not validate the certificate chain.
Workloads with many connections and small request/response traffic, where the measured gain over asio is about 5% (412K vs 393K QPS). That is too small on its own to justify a runtime switch.

Code bases with heavy use of third-party blocking libraries, OpenMP or std::thread interop. Blocking calls stall every coroutine on that vCPU, and mixing threading models has caused crashes (#137). The library is also pre-1.0 (v0.9.6); recent fixes include critical work-stealing scheduler bugs (#1245) and an io_uring use-after-free (#1270), and a rare crash in prelocked_thread_interrupt is still open (#1093).

integration.form: static lib or shared lib: the CMake targets photon_static and photon_shared, pulled in with FetchContent or a git submodule
integration.dependencies: openssl, zlib, libcurl (on by default) and libaio on Linux; liburing, libfuse, libgsasl, e2fs, F-Stack/DPDK, SPDK and rdma-core are optional; tests need gflags and googletest. PHOTON_BUILD_DEPENDENCIES=ON builds these from source.
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (PHOTON_CXX_STANDARD defaults to 14) and CMake 3.14+. CI runs GCC 8-14 on Linux (C++14 to C++23) and Apple Clang on macOS 15 (C++17).
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS on x86-64 and ARM64. The x86-64 build passes -msse4.2 -mpopcnt -mcx16. The ARM64 build passes -mcpu=generic+crc+crypto+lse, except in MinSizeRel. The io_uring engine needs kernel 5.8+ and PHOTON_ENABLE_URING=ON. Windows is not listed as supported.
integration.thread_safety: Each OS thread that calls photon::init() becomes a vCPU, and its coroutines are cooperatively scheduled and can be migrated. The docs say Photon's sync primitives and thread_interrupt are thread-safe across vCPUs. std:: locks and blocking syscalls block the whole vCPU, and non-Photon threads should hand work over through Executor or WorkPool.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false: it uses a different programming model (blocking-style coroutines over ISocketServer/ISocketStream instead of io_context plus completion handlers). photon_std:: replaces std::thread and std::mutex, not asio.

gotchas: The default coroutine stack is 8 MB (virtual memory, committed lazily), with a minimum of 16 KB plus a guard page. The docs warn that stack overflow is not detected immediately and can trample memory, so avoid deep recursion. thread_create() mallocs a stack every time; use ThreadPool or pooled_stack_allocator for short-lived coroutines.
After photon::init(), do not make blocking calls on that OS thread. One blocking read() or std::mutex wait freezes every coroutine on the vCPU.
Join is off by default, and joinable threads leak if never joined. Calling thread_join() or thread_interrupt() on a thread that has already exited core-dumps.

Build your app and Photon with the same C++ standard. Open issue #277 notes that C++14 builds make the std library act as if it were in C++17 mode (to get string_view), which causes ABI inconsistency between binaries.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Photon over libhv when you want blocking-style coroutine code plus disk I/O, RPC and HTTP in one C++ runtime rather than a callback event loop. Pick it over monoio when your code is C++; on Photon's own page it leads monoio per core (1604K vs 610K QPS streaming, 412K vs 400K ping-pong). io_uring-echo-server is a demo, not a library.
verified_claims_summary: Photon's first-party TCP echo test ran one server thread, 512-byte buffers, on 64-core 'Intel Platinum 2.70GHz' cloud VMs with kernel 6.x and a 32Gb network. With 4 streaming connections Photon reached 1604K QPS vs boost::asio's 634K (~2.5x); with 1000 ping-pong connections it reached 412K vs 393K (~1.05x). Photon used its default tcp socket on epoll and a CMake Release build (-O2 -DNDEBUG, plus SSE4.2 flags on x86-64 per CMakeLists.txt). The asio server code, the asio version and the compiler are not published.
status_note: Actively maintained: v0.9.6 came out on 2026-08-21, the last commit was on 2026-09-25, and it has used stable release branches since 0.7. It is Apache-2.0 but still pre-1.0, and it is a large CMake-built library with OpenSSL, zlib, libcurl and libaio dependencies, not something you copy in as a few files.
